# One missing value: accident, clue, or problem? {#sec-eda-missing-data}

```{r}
#| include: false

library(here)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(gt)
library(naniar)
library(visdat)
library(brms)
library(ggdist)
library(mice)

# The book's shared plot theme (this also loads the legend helpers)
Plot_theme <- source("functions/plot_theme.R")$value

# Read the cell data (one row per animal)
cell_data <- read.csv(here("project/AnalysisData/Cells_Gfap-Pdgfrb.csv"))

# Size of the table, quoted in the text
n_rows <- nrow(cell_data)
n_cols <- ncol(cell_data)

# Colorblind-safe pair (Okabe-Ito) reused across the figures of this chapter
okabe_ito <- c(observed = "#0072B2", missing = "#D55E00")
```

In @sec-eda-first-look, `skim()` told us that exactly one value in `cell_data` is missing: `Pdgfrb_Neg`, animal `Td79`. One cell out of `r n_rows * n_cols` (`r n_rows` rows times `r n_cols` columns), about `r round(100 / (n_rows * n_cols), 1)`% of the table. It would be perfectly reasonable to shrug. I did, the first time. Then I asked myself the question this chapter is built around:

::: {style="text-align: center"}
***Is this NA an accident, a clue, or a problem?***
:::

An accident is a value that went missing for a reason that has nothing to do with the biology (a dropped slide), and that costs you a little precision and nothing else. A clue is a missing value that tells you something about how the data were produced, and therefore about whether the rest of the numbers can be trusted. A problem is a missing value that, if you handle it carelessly, changes your answer. A single `NA` could in principle be any of the three, and the honest thing to say at the outset is that one cell cannot tell us which. What I can do is show you how to look, what the standard ways of thinking about missingness assume, and what each way of dealing with it costs. I should also warn you that this particular `NA` is a very small stage for a very large topic: several of the plots below will illustrate a method more than they will discover anything, and I will say so when that happens. Near the end of the chapter I borrow a real MRI dataset to show you a second, very different kind of `NA`, one that is not an accident at all, so that you can tell them apart in your own tables.

## Looking at a single missing value

When I first learned to look for missing data in R, I used `is.na()` and `colSums()`, and they work. But a table of counts is a poor way to *see* the pattern, in the same way a list of well coordinates is a poor way to see which wells of a plate failed. The packages `naniar` [@naniar] and `visdat` [@visdat] exist to draw that plate map. They treat missingness as data worth plotting in its own right, and they both return ordinary `ggplot2` objects, so everything we add on top (the book's `Plot_theme`, a colorblind-safe palette) works exactly as it does for any other figure.

Start with the most literal picture. `vis_miss()` draws the whole table as a grid, one row per animal and one column per variable, and colors each cell by whether the value is there. I like it as a first look precisely because it makes no decision for you: you see the table, with the holes (@fig-missing-vismiss). It is a heatmap of a binary variable, which is the right chart when the thing you want to locate is *where*, in two dimensions, something happens.

```{r}
#| label: fig-missing-vismiss
#| fig-cap: "Every cell of `cell_data`, colored by whether it is present. Rows are the 49 animals, columns are the 20 variables. Exactly one cell is missing: `Pdgfrb_Neg` for animal `Td79`."
#| fig-alt: "Grid of 49 rows and 20 columns. Almost every cell is the same pale color, indicating observed values. A single dark cell appears in the Pdgfrb_Neg column near the bottom of the grid."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6

# The whole table as a grid: one cell per value, coloured by present or missing
vis_miss(cell_data, show_perc = FALSE, show_perc_col = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("grey85", okabe_ito[["missing"]]),
    labels = c("Present", "Missing")
  ) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Animal (row)", fill = NULL) +
  Plot_theme +
  # Tilt the long column names so they stay readable; legend above the grid
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 60, hjust = 0, size = 10),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10),
        plot.margin = margin(5, 40, 5, 5)) +
  legend_top()
```

One orange cell in a sea of gray. This is the moment to be candid: for a dataset this size the figure adds nothing that `skim()` had not already told us. Where `vis_miss()` earns its keep is on a spreadsheet with hundreds of columns, where a missing block (every measurement from one batch of animals, say) lines up as a stripe and you see in half a second what no summary table would show. I am using it here because you should meet the tool on a dataset where you can verify every cell by eye.

The second view collapses the grid into a count per variable (@fig-missing-missvar). `gg_miss_var()` is a bar chart, and bars are the right encoding for an amount, as long as they start at zero, which these do.

```{r}
#| label: fig-missing-missvar
#| fig-cap: "Number of missing values per variable, sorted. Nineteen variables have none; `Pdgfrb_Neg` has one."
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart of the count of missing values for each variable in cell_data. Only the Pdgfrb_Neg bar has nonzero length, with a value of one."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5

# One bar per variable: how many values are missing in each
gg_miss_var(cell_data) +
  labs(y = "Missing values (count)") +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10))
```

Same lesson, a different encoding: it is a ranked list of problems, which is useful when twenty variables compete for your attention, and nearly pointless when there is a single entry on it.

The third view is the one I would keep even for this dataset, because it asks a question the first two cannot: *where in the rest of the data does the missing value sit?* `geom_miss_point()` is a scatterplot that does not throw away points with a missing coordinate. Instead it parks them on a stripe just below (or left of) the axis, in a different color, so you can ask whether the missing animal looks like its neighbors (@fig-missing-misspoint). For `Td79`, we know its `Pdgfrb_Pos` count, so we can see where it would sit in the vertical direction, even though its horizontal position is unknown. I color the missing one and also label it directly with its ID, so it stays identifiable in a grayscale printout of the PDF edition.

```{r}
#| label: fig-missing-misspoint
#| fig-cap: "`Pdgfrb_Pos` against `Pdgfrb_Neg`. The animal with a missing `Pdgfrb_Neg` (orange, labeled `Td79`) is parked just left of the observed range, at the height of its known `Pdgfrb_Pos`. That position on the horizontal axis is not data: it is a place to put the point so you can see it."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of PDGFR-beta positive cell counts on the vertical axis against PDGFR-beta negative cell counts on the horizontal axis. Blue points are scattered across the plot. One orange point labeled Td79 sits slightly to the left of the lowest horizontal value, at a vertical position near 400."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5

# Where geom_miss_point() parks the missing animal, so we can label it directly
neg_range <- range(cell_data$Pdgfrb_Neg, na.rm = TRUE)
parked <- cell_data |>
  filter(is.na(Pdgfrb_Neg)) |>
  mutate(Pdgfrb_Neg = neg_range[1] - 0.1 * diff(neg_range))   # naniar's default stripe

# Scatter plot that keeps the point with a missing x, parked just left of the axis
ggplot(cell_data, aes(x = Pdgfrb_Neg, y = Pdgfrb_Pos)) +
  geom_miss_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.85) +
  # Label the missing animal directly with its ID
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = parked, aes(label = MouseID),
                           nudge_y = 500, size = 5, color = okabe_ito[["missing"]],
                           min.segment.length = 0) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Missing" = okabe_ito[["missing"]],
                                "Not Missing" = okabe_ito[["observed"]])) +
  labs(x = "PDGFR-β negative cells (Pdgfrb_Neg)",
       y = "PDGFR-β positive cells (Pdgfrb_Pos)",
       color = NULL) +
  Plot_theme +
  legend_top()
```

There is nothing odd about where the triangle sits vertically: a count near 400 is unremarkable for `Pdgfrb_Pos`, and the day-3 animals cluster at low counts anyway. That is mildly reassuring and, with one point, proves nothing.

One more `naniar` function deserves a mention because it is the one everyone wants to try. `gg_miss_upset()` draws an UpSet plot: it counts how often *combinations* of variables are missing together, which is the right question when many variables go missing in patterns (a failed channel takes three measurements with it). Let me run it, because the result is itself informative.

```{r}
#| label: miss-upset-attempt

# Try the UpSet plot and print the error message instead of stopping the render
tryCatch(
  gg_miss_upset(cell_data),
  error = function(e) cat(conditionMessage(e))
)
```

It refuses, and for a sound reason: a combination needs at least two variables with missing values, and we have one. I would rather show you the error than draw an empty plot. The takeaway is that `gg_miss_upset()` is a tool for the day your dataset has many `NA`s in several columns, and for that day you now know it exists. That day arrives in @sec-missing-structural, where the same function works.

### The clue hiding in a derived column

So far the missing value looks like a small, isolated accident. Before accepting that, I asked a different question, one that no missing-data plot suggests: *what depends on this column?* A value that is blank in the raw file can still leave a fingerprint in every column computed from it. `Pdgfrb_Total` is the natural suspect, since the name says it is the sum of the positive and negative counts.

```{r}
#| label: check-total

# Do Pos + Neg and Total agree in every row where Neg is present?
with(subset(cell_data, !is.na(Pdgfrb_Neg)),
     all(Pdgfrb_Pos + Pdgfrb_Neg == Pdgfrb_Total))

# And what does the animal with the missing Neg look like?
cell_data |>
  filter(is.na(Pdgfrb_Neg)) |>
  select(MouseID, DPI, Pdgfrb_Pos, Pdgfrb_Neg, Pdgfrb_Total)

# Number of animals with a recorded Pdgfrb_Neg, quoted in the text
n_neg_present <- sum(!is.na(cell_data$Pdgfrb_Neg))
```

In all `r n_neg_present` animals with a recorded `Pdgfrb_Neg`, `Pdgfrb_Pos + Pdgfrb_Neg` equals `Pdgfrb_Total` exactly. Animal `Td79` is the exception that matters: its `Pdgfrb_Total` is 398, identical to its `Pdgfrb_Pos`, and **not** `NA`. Whoever (or whatever spreadsheet formula) computed the total treated the missing negative count as zero. Think of a plate reader that, faced with an empty well, reports an absorbance of zero instead of "no reading": the column looks complete, and it is quietly wrong (@fig-missing-plate).

![An empty well is not a reading of zero. A column that reports 0 for "nothing there" looks complete, and is quietly wrong.](images/eda-missing-data_empty-well-reads-zero.png){#fig-missing-plate fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of a microplate on a wooden bench with rows of teal-filled wells and one empty, pale well near the middle. Beside it, a small analog dial rests its needle near the zero mark with a faint green glow, and a pipette lies in front of the plate."}

This is the first real finding of the chapter, and it answers the opening question in a way I did not expect. The `NA` itself is small. The *derived* value built on it is not an `NA` at all, it is a wrong number that looks fine, and it propagates. Any analysis that uses `Pdgfrb_Total`, for instance a proportion `Pdgfrb_Pos / Pdgfrb_Total`, will see this animal as having a PDGFR-β+ share of exactly 100%, which is false unless that animal really had no negative cells (its share is below 100% by whatever the missing negative count was; @sec-missing-data-measurement-error returns to the possibility that the count is truly zero). I will come back to the consequence for the proportion model in @sec-logistic-regression in the take-home message. For now, notice the habit this suggests: when a column has an `NA`, check every column that was computed from it.

## Three ways a value can go missing

Knowing that a value is missing is half of the problem. The other half is *why*, because the reason decides which analyses are safe. Statisticians sort the reasons into three mechanisms, and I will give you the lab versions first, since you have met all three at the bench.

**The accident.** A rack of tubes is dropped on the floor on a Tuesday afternoon. Which samples are lost has nothing to do with the animal, the day, the treatment or the value you would have measured. Whatever is missing is a random draw from what you had. This is the optimistic case.

**The explained loss.** Sections from the day-3 brains are softer after the ischemic insult and tear more often when you cut them. Now the losses are not random: they are concentrated at day 3. But notice what saves you. *You know which animals were day 3*, because you recorded it. The missingness is explained by something you measured, and within the day-3 animals, which ones tore is no more likely to depend on how many cells they had.

**The informative loss.** The most severe infarcts have a core that crumbles when you cut it, so the sections you could not quantify are *precisely* the ones with the most damage. Or, closer to a familiar problem in survival experiments: the animals that did not make it to day 30 are the ones with the largest lesions, so the day-30 group you analyze is a self-selected survivor group. Here the reason a value is missing is the value itself. This is the nightmare case, because the data you have are a biased sample of the data you wanted, and nothing in the data you have says so (@fig-missing-net).

![A wide-mesh net only keeps the big fish, so every fish you hold looks big. When what's lost depends on the value itself, the data you kept are a biased sample, and nothing in them says so.](images/eda-missing-data_wide-mesh-net.png){#fig-missing-net fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of a smiling researcher in a lab coat and green sweater holding a wide-mesh fishing net at the edge of a pond. Three large teal fish are inside the net, while many small ochre fish slip through its holes and leap into the water below."}

Rubin gave these three situations names [@jamshidian2009; @harrell2015]. Let $Y$ be the full set of measurements, which splits into the part you observed, $Y_{\text{obs}}$, and the part that is missing, $Y_{\text{mis}}$. Let $R$ be an indicator that is 1 when a value was observed and 0 when it was lost, and let $\phi$ stand for whatever parameters govern the loss process. The three mechanisms differ in what the probability of being missing is allowed to depend on.

The accident is [missing completely at random]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} (MCAR): the chance of loss does not depend on anything in the data.

$$
P(R \mid Y_{\text{obs}}, Y_{\text{mis}}, \phi) = P(R \mid \phi)
$$ {#eq-mcar}

The explained loss is [missing at random]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} (MAR): once you account for what you observed, the chance of loss no longer depends on the values you did not see.

$$
P(R \mid Y_{\text{obs}}, Y_{\text{mis}}, \phi) = P(R \mid Y_{\text{obs}}, \phi)
$$ {#eq-mar}

The informative loss is [missing not at random]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} (MNAR): the chance of loss depends on $Y_{\text{mis}}$ itself, even after accounting for everything you observed.

$$
P(R \mid Y_{\text{obs}}, Y_{\text{mis}}, \phi) \text{ depends on } Y_{\text{mis}}
$$ {#eq-mnar}

The name "missing at random" is, I think, the worst piece of terminology in this field, because the data are *not* missing at random in the everyday sense; they are missing for reasons that you happen to have recorded. It helps to read @eq-mar as "missing, at random, *given what I measured*".

::: callout-tip
### MAR is a property of your model, not of your column

This is the subtlety that makes the three labels slippery. A column that is MNAR when you ignore the other variables can become MAR once you include the right ones. If the crumbling sections are the ones from big infarcts and you have measured infarct volume, then conditioning on infarct volume can turn an informative loss into an explained one. The label depends on which variables are in the analysis [@harrell2015]. It is also why the work of building a good model for missing data is mostly the work of thinking about *how the data were produced*.
:::

### Can the data tell us which one we have?

I wish the answer were yes. It is partly. You can often detect that missingness is *not* completely random: compare the observed variables between rows with and without a missing value (the day, the condition, the area), and if the groups differ, MCAR is in trouble. Formal versions of this exist, such as Little's MCAR test [@jamshidian2009]. What you cannot do, from the observed data alone, is distinguish MAR from MNAR, because the thing that would settle it, the missing value, is exactly the thing you do not have [@harrell2015; @gelman2020].

With one missing value in 49 rows, even the first comparison is out of reach. We would be comparing a group of 48 animals against a group of one, and a sample of one has no variance to estimate. So here is where the book has to be honest about how little the data can say. All I can offer from the table is a description: `Td79` is a day-3 MCAO animal, whose `Pdgfrb_Pos` count is ordinary, and 1 of the 8 day-3 animals is missing, 0 of 41 at any other day. That is a pattern with a sample size of one, and I would not build a story on it.

What *can* settle the question is knowledge of how the data were produced, which is information from outside the table. If I were analyzing this for a paper I would do three things, in this order. I would ask whoever quantified the sections what happened to `Td79` (a torn section, a failed stain, a blank in the export?), and write the answer next to the cleaning code. I would check whether the same person or batch has other quirks. And, as the next section shows, I would run the analysis a few different ways, including some deliberately pessimistic ones, to see whether anything changes. The `Pdgfrb_Total` clue points toward the first of those explanations being a blank in an export, not a lost slide, since a lost slide would more plausibly have taken `Pdgfrb_Pos` with it. But that is a story that I made up to fit the pattern, in the same spirit as the area-unit story of @sec-eda-data-quality. It is a hypothesis, and the lab notes would say if it is true.

### What the mechanisms do to an estimate

The three definitions are abstract until you watch them bias something, and with one missing value I cannot show you that on `cell_data`. So I will use a small simulation, the kind of generative check @sec-bayesian-core-workflow argued for, where *I* know the truth. I generate 200 measurements $y$ that depend on a recorded variable $z$ (think of $z$ as the day, and $y$ as a cell count), with a true mean of 2. Then I delete about 30% of the $y$ values by each of the three mechanisms: at random, depending on $z$ (the explained loss), and depending on $y$ itself (the informative loss). I estimate the mean of $y$ two ways: from the complete cases only, and from a regression of $y$ on $z$ fitted to the complete cases and then averaged over *all* the $z$ values (this is a stand-in for any method that uses what we recorded about the animals with missing data). I repeat this a thousand times and plot where the estimates land.

I show the spread across simulations as a dot with an interval, and the truth as a vertical line: the question is whether the line lies inside the cloud of estimates. I encode the method with both color and shape (@fig-missing-mechanisms).

```{r}
#| label: fig-missing-mechanisms
#| fig-cap: "Estimated mean of `y` (truth = 2, vertical line) over 1000 simulated datasets, for three missingness mechanisms and two estimators. Dots are the average estimate; bars cover the middle 95% of estimates across simulations. About 30% of `y` is deleted in each scenario."
#| fig-alt: "Three stacked panels, one per mechanism: MCAR, MAR, and MNAR. In each, two estimators are shown as a dot with a horizontal bar. In the MCAR panel both estimators sit on the vertical line at 2. In the MAR panel the complete-case estimator sits well to the left of the line while the model-based estimator sits on it. In the MNAR panel both estimators sit to the left of the line."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5

# Fixed seed so the simulation is identical on every render
set.seed(2026)

# One simulated dataset: z is recorded, y depends on z, then ~30% of y is deleted
# under each mechanism (random; depending on z; depending on y itself)
one_sim <- function(n = 200) {
  z <- rnorm(n)
  y <- 2 + 1.5 * z + rnorm(n)
  p_mcar <- rep(0.30, n)
  p_mar  <- plogis(-0.85 + 1.5 * z)
  p_mnar <- plogis(-0.85 + 1.5 * (y - 2) / 1.8)

  # Delete values with probability p, then estimate the mean of y two ways
  est <- function(p, mech) {
    miss <- runif(n) < p
    d <- data.frame(y = y, z = z)[!miss, ]
    c(mech = mech,
      `Complete cases` = mean(d$y),
      `Uses recorded z` = mean(predict(lm(y ~ z, d), newdata = data.frame(z = z))))
  }
  rbind(est(p_mcar, "MCAR"), est(p_mar, "MAR"), est(p_mnar, "MNAR"))
}

# Repeat 1000 times and summarize: mean estimate and middle 95% per mechanism and method
sims <- do.call(rbind, replicate(1000, one_sim(), simplify = FALSE)) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-mech, names_to = "method", values_to = "estimate") |>
  mutate(estimate = as.numeric(estimate),
         mech = factor(mech, levels = c("MCAR", "MAR", "MNAR"))) |>
  group_by(mech, method) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(estimate),
            lo = quantile(estimate, 0.025),
            hi = quantile(estimate, 0.975),
            .groups = "drop")

# One panel per mechanism; dashed line = the true mean we planted (2)
ggplot(sims, aes(x = mean, y = method, color = method, shape = method)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), size = 0.8, linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~mech, ncol = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Complete cases" = "#E69F00",
                                "Uses recorded z" = "#0072B2")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Complete cases" = 16, "Uses recorded z" = 17)) +
  labs(x = "Estimated mean of y", y = NULL) +
  Plot_theme +
  # Rows are labelled on the axis, so no legend is needed
  legend_none() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"))
```

Read it from top to bottom. Under MCAR, both estimators land on the truth: throwing away a random 30% of the animals costs you precision (the bars are wider than they would be with everything) but not accuracy. Under MAR, the complete-case mean is wrong, and by a lot, because the animals with a high $z$ are lost more often and they are also the ones with a high $y$; the estimator that uses the recorded $z$ repairs it. Under MNAR, *both* are wrong, and neither tells you that. This is the figure I would put on a slide titled "why the mechanism matters": the choice of method is only as good as the assumption about how the values were lost, and the assumption cannot be read off the data.

## Missing by design: a second kind of NA {#sec-missing-structural}

Every missing value so far has been a value that *exists* and was not recorded. Animal `Td79` has a number of PDGFR-β-negative cells; it just did not make it into the spreadsheet. There is a second kind of `NA` that looks identical in the table and asks for a completely different response, and I would like you to meet it before you meet it in your own data. Picture a table with ischemic and sham animals and a column for infarct volume. Every sham animal has an `NA` there, and nobody dropped a slide: there is no infarct to measure. Asking a sham mouse for its lesion volume is like asking a naive cage-mate for its latency to find a platform it has never been trained on. The value is not lost, it does not exist. I will call this [structural missingness]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}: the `NA` is produced by the design of the study, by a variable you recorded, and not by a mishap.

`cell_data` has no example of this, so I borrow a real one. The R package `NeuroDataSets` [@neurodatasets] ships `OASIS_cross_tbl_df`, the cross-sectional release of the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies [@marcus2007]: structural MRI and clinical assessments of 416 people aged 18 to 96, plus 20 of them scanned a second time, for 436 rows. I use it only for this section. The columns that matter here are `Age`, `Educ` (education, in five categories), `SES` (socioeconomic status, five categories), `MMSE` (Mini-Mental State Examination, a cognitive screening score), `CDR` (Clinical Dementia Rating: 0 none, 0.5 very mild, 1 mild, 2 moderate), `nWBV` (the volume of the brain as a fraction of the intracranial volume) and `Delay` (days between the two scans of the same person).

```{r}
#| label: load-oasis

library(NeuroDataSets)

# Real MRI and clinical table (OASIS-1) shipped with the NeuroDataSets package
data("OASIS_cross_tbl_df", package = "NeuroDataSets")
oasis <- as.data.frame(OASIS_cross_tbl_df)

# Numbers quoted in the text below
n_oasis   <- nrow(oasis)
n_people  <- length(unique(sub("_MR[0-9]+$", "", oasis$ID)))
no_clinic <- is.na(oasis$CDR)                  # CDR not recorded
n_block   <- sum(no_clinic)

# Are CDR, MMSE and Educ missing in exactly the same rows?
same_rows <- all(no_clinic == is.na(oasis$MMSE) & no_clinic == is.na(oasis$Educ))
```

I look at it the way we looked at `cell_data`: first the whole table as a grid. Here I ask `vis_miss()` to cluster the rows that share a pattern of missingness (`cluster = TRUE`), because with `r n_oasis` rows I want similar rows next to each other and not scattered in file order (@fig-missing-oasis-vismiss).

```{r}
#| label: fig-missing-oasis-vismiss
#| fig-cap: "The OASIS-1 table as a grid, rows clustered by their pattern of missingness. Dark cells are missing. Education, SES, MMSE and CDR are missing together in one large block of rows; SES alone is missing in a smaller set."
#| fig-alt: "Grid of 436 rows and 12 columns. Most cells are pale. In the columns Educ, MMSE and CDR, a large block of about 200 rows at one end is dark; the SES column is dark for those same rows and for a short additional stretch of about twenty rows."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6

# Whole table, rows grouped by missingness pattern; dark orange = missing
vis_miss(oasis, cluster = TRUE, show_perc = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("grey85", okabe_ito[["missing"]]),
    labels = c("Present", "Missing")
  ) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Row (clustered)", fill = NULL) +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 60, hjust = 0, size = 10),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10),
        plot.margin = margin(5, 40, 5, 5)) +
  legend_top()
```

This time the grid *does* discover something, and the contrast with @fig-missing-vismiss is the point of the section. There is no lone orange cell to hunt for: there is a slab. `r n_block` of the `r n_oasis` rows (`r round(100 * n_block / n_oasis)`%) have no `CDR`, and they are the same rows that have no `MMSE` and no `Educ` (are the three columns missing together in every one of them? `r same_rows`). `SES` is missing in those rows too, and in a few more. When several columns go dark in exactly the same rows, you are rarely looking at several accidents. You are looking at one decision.

The tool built for that question is the UpSet plot, which I could not use on `cell_data`. It counts how often each *combination* of missing variables occurs (@fig-missing-oasis-upset).

::: callout-tip
### How to read this figure

Read it from the bottom matrix up. Each column of dots is one *combination* of variables: a filled dot means "missing in this combination", and dots joined by a line are missing together. The bar above a column says how many rows have exactly that combination, and the small bars on the left give the total missing per variable. Look for tall bars with several joined dots: that is a block that fails as a unit. Short bars with a single dot are the ordinary, isolated `NA`s.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-missing-oasis-upset
#| fig-cap: "Combinations of missing variables in OASIS-1. The tall bar is the block of rows missing Educ, MMSE, CDR and SES together; the short bar is SES missing on its own."
#| fig-alt: "UpSet plot. The tallest bar, about 200, joins four dots for the variables CDR, MMSE, Educ and SES. A much shorter bar of about 19 has a single dot for SES. Horizontal bars on the left show 220 missing for SES and 201 each for Educ, MMSE and CDR."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5

# Count each combination of missing variables (drawn with the UpSetR package)
gg_miss_upset(oasis, main.bar.color = okabe_ito[["observed"]],
              sets.bar.color = okabe_ito[["observed"]], text.scale = 1.4)
```

Two combinations explain the whole table: a block of `r n_block` rows where four variables are missing together, and `r sum(is.na(oasis$SES) & !no_clinic)` rows where only `SES` is missing. They are different problems, and I take them one at a time, starting with the block. What decides which rows are in it? The first suspect is whatever the study recorded about each person, and the obvious candidate is `Age` (@fig-missing-oasis-age).

```{r}
#| label: fig-missing-oasis-age
#| fig-cap: "People in OASIS-1 by age band, split by whether the clinical rating (CDR) was recorded. Numbers inside the bars are counts (the two people in their thirties with a rating are too few to label). Every person under 30 lacks it; every person aged 60 or over has it."
#| fig-alt: "Stacked bar chart with seven age bands from 18-29 to 80-96. In the 18-29 band all 157 people are in the orange group without a clinical rating. The orange share shrinks across the 30s, 40s and 50s, and from 60 onward all bars are entirely blue, meaning a rating was recorded."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.5

# Count people per age band, by CDR recorded or not
age_bands <- oasis |>
  mutate(band = cut(Age, c(17, 29, 39, 49, 59, 69, 79, 100),
                    labels = c("18-29", "30-39", "40-49", "50-59",
                               "60-69", "70-79", "80-96")),
         status = ifelse(is.na(CDR), "CDR not recorded", "CDR recorded")) |>
  count(band, status)

# Stacked bars from zero (an amount per band) with the counts written inside
ggplot(age_bands, aes(x = band, y = n, fill = status)) +
  geom_col(color = "black", linewidth = 0.4) +
  # Label only segments tall enough to hold a number
  geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(n >= 5, n, "")),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), size = 5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("CDR recorded" = okabe_ito[["observed"]],
                               "CDR not recorded" = okabe_ito[["missing"]])) +
  labs(x = "Age band (years)", y = "People (rows)", fill = NULL) +
  Plot_theme +
  legend_inside(0.70, 0.85)
```

@fig-missing-oasis-age is the answer. The block is not scattered at random: it is the young. Nobody under 30 has a rating (`r sum(oasis$Age < 30 & no_clinic)` of `r sum(oasis$Age < 30)`), only two people in their thirties do, and from 60 onward everybody does (`r sum(oasis$Age >= 60 & !no_clinic)` of `r sum(oasis$Age >= 60)`). The `r sum(oasis$Age < 60 & !no_clinic)` people younger than 60 who *do* have a rating all have `CDR` equal to 0, that is, no dementia. I read this as a study in which the clinical assessment was collected where dementia could plausibly be present and left blank for most healthy young adults. That is my reading of the pattern, not a documented rule; the description of the release [@marcus2007] is where I would confirm the exact criterion before putting it in a methods section.

Whatever the exact rule, the nature of the `NA` is clear. The probability of being missing is close to a function of a variable we *did* record, `Age`. In the vocabulary of @eq-mar this is as MAR as it gets: given what we observed, the missingness has nothing left to say about the unseen value. And yet that does not rescue you, and the reason is the most useful idea of this section.

### Why you cannot fill these in

The MAR argument licenses imputation *when the values you would borrow from exist*. For a 20-year-old with no `CDR`, an imputation model must borrow from people like them who *do* have a `CDR`, and there is nobody: the youngest person with a recorded rating is `r min(oasis$Age[!no_clinic])`, and `r sum(oasis$Age < min(oasis$Age[!no_clinic]))` rows are younger than that. Any method (`mice`, `mi()`, anything) would be extrapolating from people in their seventies to people in their twenties, and would hand back a number for every young adult that looks like data and is not. When the missingness is a function of a variable and the observed rows do not overlap the missing ones in that variable, the data hold no information about what the values *would* have been, and no amount of modeling creates it.

Complete-case analysis has the opposite problem, and it is quieter. Dropping rows with an `NA` is not neutral here: it changes who the analysis is about. @tbl-missing-two-groups shows how different the two groups of rows are.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-missing-two-groups
#| tbl-cap: "The rows that have a clinical rating and the rows that do not are two different populations. Any analysis of CDR, MMSE or education done on complete cases describes only the first."

# Compare the two groups of rows on age and on brain volume (nWBV is never missing)
oasis |>
  mutate(Group = ifelse(is.na(CDR), "CDR not recorded", "CDR recorded")) |>
  group_by(Group) |>
  summarise(Rows = n(),
            `Median age` = median(Age),
            `Age range` = paste(min(Age), max(Age), sep = " to "),
            `Mean nWBV` = round(mean(nWBV), 3)) |>
  gt()
```

The complete cases are people with a median age in the seventies; the rest are people in their twenties. The brain volume fraction `nWBV` is recorded for everyone, and it differs between the groups (`r round(mean(oasis$nWBV[!no_clinic]), 2)` against `r round(mean(oasis$nWBV[no_clinic]), 2)`), because it falls with age. A study that related `nWBV` to `CDR` on the complete cases would be a study of older adults, and its conclusions would not extend to the young, with or without a missing-data package.

So what *do* you do with a structural `NA`? Not impute, and not drop silently. You change the question, or the population, to match what exists. Either you restrict the analysis to the rows where the variable is defined (here, adults aged 60 or over, where the rating is always present) and say so in the title of the analysis; or you analyze only the variables that exist for everyone (`Age`, `nWBV`, `eTIV`); or you model the two parts separately. What you must not do is let a default (`na.omit`, an imputation routine) make that decision for you without telling the reader.

### The ordinary NAs next to the structural ones

The second combination in @fig-missing-oasis-upset, `SES` missing on its own, is a different animal, and it looks like `Td79`'s cousin: a value that should exist and does not. There are `r sum(is.na(oasis$SES) & !no_clinic)` of them, all in people who have a clinical rating. With 19 rows, and not 1, I can finally do what I could not do for `Td79`: ask whether the missing values are related to something I observed. @tbl-missing-ses cross-tabulates them with the clinical rating.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-missing-ses
#| tbl-cap: "Among people with a clinical rating, how often SES is missing, by CDR. Missing SES is rare in people without dementia and much more common in people with a rating above 0."

# Among rows with a CDR, count how many lack SES, per CDR level
oasis |>
  filter(!is.na(CDR)) |>
  group_by(CDR) |>
  summarise(People = n(),
            `SES missing` = sum(is.na(SES)),
            `% missing` = round(100 * mean(is.na(SES)), 1)) |>
  gt()
```

```{r}
#| label: ses-facts
#| include: false

# Rows with CDR 0 and rows with CDR above 0, for the numbers in the text
ses_cdr0 <- oasis |> filter(CDR == 0)
ses_cdrp <- oasis |> filter(CDR > 0)
```

The pattern is clear enough to say something: `SES` is missing in `r sum(is.na(ses_cdr0$SES))` of `r nrow(ses_cdr0)` people with `CDR` 0 (`r round(100 * mean(is.na(ses_cdr0$SES)), 1)`%) and in `r sum(is.na(ses_cdrp$SES))` of `r nrow(ses_cdrp)` people with `CDR` above 0 (`r round(100 * mean(is.na(ses_cdrp$SES)), 1)`%). So these `NA`s are *not* MCAR: they depend on something observed. That is the situation where the machinery of the next section is appropriate, provided the imputation model includes the rating (and age and education) so that the dependence is accounted for, which is exactly the MAR bet. What the table cannot tell you is whether, within a given `CDR`, people with a lower or higher unseen `SES` were the ones left blank. That is the MNAR question and, as before, only the study's procedures can answer it.

### An NA that `is.na()` cannot see

One more structural `NA` hides in plain sight, and it is the sneakiest. `Delay`, the days between two scans, is recorded for the people who were scanned twice. Everyone else has the text `"N/A"`. Because it is text and not a true `NA`, `is.na()` reports zero missing values in the whole column, and every plot in this section so far has treated it as complete. `naniar` has a function for exactly this: `miss_scan_count()` searches columns for strings that *mean* missing, and `replace_with_na()` converts them.

```{r}
#| label: oasis-delay

# Before: is.na() sees nothing, because "N/A" is text
sum(is.na(oasis$Delay))

# Count how many cells hold the string "N/A" in each column
miss_scan_count(oasis, search = list("N/A")) |> filter(n > 0)

# Convert the string into a real NA and count again
oasis <- oasis |> replace_with_na(replace = list(Delay = "N/A"))
sum(is.na(oasis$Delay))
```

This is structural in the strictest sense: a second scan did not happen, so there is no delay to record. I mention it for one more reason. The `r sum(!is.na(oasis$Delay))` rows that do have a `Delay` belong to people who already appear earlier in the table (their IDs end in `_MR2`), so the table has `r n_oasis` rows but only `r n_people` people. Rows are not independent observations of different individuals, a fact that the `NA` pattern gave away and that matters for every model that treats a row as a person. Keep it in mind for the chapters on repeated measurements later in the book.

@tbl-missing-two-kinds puts the kinds side by side, since the whole point of this section is that you need to tell them apart before you pick a tool.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-missing-two-kinds
#| tbl-cap: "The single NA of `cell_data` and the two kinds of NA in OASIS-1 are different problems."

# One column per kind of NA; the rows are questions to ask of any NA
tibble::tribble(
  ~Question, ~`Td79 in cell_data`, ~`CDR, MMSE, Educ in OASIS-1`, ~`SES alone in OASIS-1`,
  "Does the value exist?", "Yes, it was not recorded", "No, not assessed by design", "Yes, it was not recorded",
  "How many?", "1 of 49 animals", "201 of 436 rows", "19 of 235 rows with a CDR",
  "What explains it?", "Unknown (lab notes)", "Age, which we recorded", "Partly CDR, which we recorded",
  "Can we impute it?", "Yes, little is at stake", "No, nothing to borrow from", "Yes, if CDR and age are in the model",
  "What to do?", "Complete cases or imputation, report both", "Change the population or the question", "Impute under MAR, with a sensitivity check"
) |>
  gt()
```

::: {.callout-note title="How to report it"}
**Methods.** The clinical rating (CDR), the cognitive score (MMSE) and education were not recorded for `r n_block` of `r n_oasis` rows (`r round(100 * n_block / n_oasis)`%), all of them people aged 58 or younger, and their absence follows age: no person under 30 has them and every person aged 60 or over does. Because there are no recorded values at these ages from which to impute, we did not impute them; analyses involving these variables were restricted to the `r sum(oasis$Age >= 60)` participants aged 60 or older. The text `"N/A"` in the scan-delay column was recoded as missing, and the `r sum(!is.na(oasis$Delay))` repeat scans were identified as belonging to people already in the table.

**Results.** Among people with a recorded rating, SES was missing in `r round(100 * mean(is.na(ses_cdr0$SES)), 1)`% of those with CDR 0 and `r round(100 * mean(is.na(ses_cdrp$SES)), 1)`% of those with CDR above 0, so we modeled the missing SES conditional on rating, age and education.
:::

## What to do about it

Now the practical question. Faced with a missing value, you have two broad families of options. You can **drop** the incomplete row and analyze the complete cases, or you can **keep** it and let the analysis account for what is unknown, either by filling in plausible values or by treating the unknown as a quantity to be estimated. I do not think any of these is *the* correct answer, and I would be suspicious of a book that claimed so. Each one is a different bet about the data, and the useful skill is to be able to say which bet you are making. @tbl-missing-options lays them side by side.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-missing-options
#| tbl-cap: "Four ways to handle one missing predictor, and what each one assumes. The right-hand column is the price you pay if the assumption is wrong."

# The four approaches, side by side, as a table
tibble::tribble(
  ~Approach, ~`What it does`, ~`Valid when`, ~`If the assumption fails`,
  "Complete cases (drop the row)",
    "Analyzes only animals with every variable observed.",
    "Missingness is MCAR (or depends only on the predictors, not on the outcome).",
    "Biased estimates, not just lost precision, as in the MAR panel of the figure.",
  "Multiple imputation (`mice`)",
    "Fills each gap with several plausible values drawn from a model, fits the analysis on each completed dataset, and pools the results.",
    "MAR, and the imputation model includes the outcome and the variables that explain the loss.",
    "Biased if the imputation model leaves out a relevant variable, or the loss is MNAR.",
  "Imputation inside the model (`brms` with `mi()`)",
    "Treats each missing value as an unknown parameter, estimated jointly with the regression, with a sub-model for the variable that has gaps.",
    "MAR, and the distribution you assume for the incomplete variable is reasonable.",
    "Biased under MNAR, and sensitive to a poor sub-model (including one that predicts impossible values).",
  "Sensitivity analysis (plug in extremes)",
    "Fills the gap with a low and a high plausible value and checks whether the conclusion moves.",
    "Never 'valid': it is a stress test, useful whatever the mechanism.",
    "Does not apply: it does not claim to estimate the truth, only to bound how much the answer could move."
) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(13))
```

The honest summary of that table, and of the textbooks behind it, is that when the fraction of rows with a missing value is tiny, the choice barely matters. Harrell's rule of thumb is that below about 3% of cases with any missing value it makes little difference how you impute, and complete-case analysis is an acceptable option [@harrell2015]. Huntington-Klein makes the same practical point: when the problem is a tiny fraction of the data, the extra complexity of the more sophisticated methods may cost more than it buys [@huntingtonklein2021]. We have 1 row in 49, about 2%. I am going to run all four approaches anyway, not because I expect different answers, but because *seeing* that they agree on a tiny problem is the best way to understand what they would do on a large one.

### A question to ask with the missing predictor

I need a model with an inferential question, and I want to state it in plain language first. `Pdgfrb_Neg` is the count of cells in the region that do **not** express PDGFR-β, a rough measure of how cellular that section is. The question I will ask is: *does knowing the number of PDGFR-β-negative cells tell me anything about the number of PDGFR-β-positive cells, once I know the day?* It is a deliberately modest question, picked because the missing value sits in a *predictor*, and a missing predictor is the case where the choice of method matters, whereas a missing outcome in a standard regression can simply be dropped without bias when the outcome is MAR [@gelman2020]. Treat the model as a vehicle for comparing methods, not as a scientific finding about pericytes.

Two choices to explain. I model the log of `Pdgfrb_Pos`, because the counts are positive and strongly right-skewed; a Gaussian model on the log scale, with a coefficient for each day (`DPI_f`, as in the later chapters), keeps this chapter on the linear model you already know from @sec-intro-applied-modeling. A proper count model is the subject of @sec-count-regression, and nothing about the missing-data logic changes when you swap the likelihood. And I rescale `Pdgfrb_Neg` to hundreds of cells (`neg_100`), so that the coefficient reads as "the change in log count for each 100 more negative cells", on a scale the sampler finds comfortable.

```{r}
#| label: prep-model-data

# Prepare the variables for the model
cell_data$DPI_f   <- factor(cell_data$DPI)
cell_data$log_pos <- log(cell_data$Pdgfrb_Pos)
cell_data$neg_100 <- cell_data$Pdgfrb_Neg / 100   # hundreds of cells

complete_rows <- cell_data[!is.na(cell_data$neg_100), ]   # 48 animals
nrow(complete_rows)
```

The four tabs below fit the same regression four ways. Read them with the table above in mind: the first and third drop `Td79`, the second and fourth keep it, and they keep it by different routes. In `brms`, the `mi()` term turns the missing `neg_100` into a parameter, and the second formula, `neg_100 | mi() ~ DPI_f`, is the sub-model that says what we believe about the variable that has the gap: its mean may differ by day, and the day is observed for everyone. That sub-model is where the MAR assumption lives, because it uses what we know (the day) to guess what we do not. `mice` takes the other route, drawing several completed datasets from a similar model (a normal-theory imputation of `neg_100`, using the day *and* the outcome `log_pos`, which is what the textbooks require for an unbiased slope [@harrell2015]) and pooling the 20 resulting fits with Rubin's rules [@mice]. I leave the `brms` priors at their defaults, for the same reason as in the earlier chapters: I want the data to shape the coefficients while we learn the structure.

::: panel-tabset
### brms: complete cases

```{r}
#| label: fit-brms-cc

# Bayesian fit on the 48 complete animals (cached in models/)
fit_cc <- brm(
  log_pos ~ DPI_f + neg_100,
  data = complete_rows,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/eda-missing-data_fit1.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)

summary(fit_cc)
```

### brms: `mi()`

```{r}
#| label: fit-brms-mi

# Bayesian fit on all 49 animals: mi() treats the missing neg_100 as a parameter,
# with its own sub-model (second formula) saying how neg_100 varies by day
fit_mi <- brm(
  bf(log_pos ~ DPI_f + mi(neg_100)) +
    bf(neg_100 | mi() ~ DPI_f) +
    set_rescor(FALSE),
  data = cell_data,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/eda-missing-data_fit2.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)

summary(fit_mi)
```

### lm: complete cases

```{r}
#| label: fit-lm-cc

library(parsnip)

# Ordinary least squares on the complete animals
lm_cc <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm") |>
  fit(log_pos ~ DPI_f + neg_100, data = complete_rows)

tidy(lm_cc, conf.int = TRUE)
```

### mice + lm

```{r}
#| label: fit-mice

# Multiple imputation: 20 completed datasets, normal model for neg_100
imp <- mice(
  cell_data[, c("log_pos", "DPI_f", "neg_100")],
  m = 20,
  method = c("", "", "norm"),
  seed = 123,
  printFlag = FALSE
)

# Fit the regression on each completed dataset, then pool with Rubin's rules
fits_mice <- with(imp, lm(log_pos ~ DPI_f + neg_100))
pooled <- summary(pool(fits_mice), conf.int = TRUE)
pooled
```
:::

The first thing to check, as always, is that the sampler behaved. For the `mi()` model, the largest Rhat across all parameters is `r round(max(rhat(fit_mi), na.rm = TRUE), 3)`, the smallest bulk effective sample size is `r round(min(summary(fit_mi)$fixed$Bulk_ESS, summary(fit_mi)$spec_pars$Bulk_ESS))`, and the number of divergent transitions is `r sum(nuts_params(fit_mi)$Value[nuts_params(fit_mi)$Parameter == "divergent__"])`. That meets the thresholds from the earlier chapters.

Now the comparison that the whole section was building toward. The coefficient of interest is the one for the number of negative cells, and the question is whether dropping `Td79`, imputing it inside the model, or imputing it with `mice` changes what we would conclude. I add two rows that are not methods at all, but stress tests of the kind the textbooks recommend when the mechanism is in doubt [@jamshidian2009; @harrell2015]: I fill the one gap with the *smallest* and then the *largest* `Pdgfrb_Neg` observed anywhere, refit, and see whether the coefficient moves. The intervals for those two rows are conditional on a guess, so I draw them with a different shape and do not read them as honest uncertainty. @fig-missing-compare shows all six. Each estimate is a dot with an interval (`geom_pointrange()`), not a bar, because a coefficient is a position on a line where zero means no association, not an amount that starts at zero; a bar from zero would make the smallest coefficient look like no result and the largest like a finding.

```{r}
#| label: fig-missing-compare
#| fig-cap: "Coefficient for `Pdgfrb_Neg` (per 100 more negative cells, on the log scale of `Pdgfrb_Pos`) under six ways of treating the one missing value. Points are posterior medians or estimates; bars are 95% credible or confidence intervals. The two sensitivity rows plug in the smallest and largest observed value and are conditional on that guess."
#| fig-alt: "Dot and interval plot with six rows, each giving an estimate of the same coefficient with a horizontal interval. All six dots sit between about 0.02 and 0.06 and all six intervals cross zero. The two sensitivity rows use a different shape."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.2

# Pull the neg_100 coefficient and its interval from each of the four fits
b_cc <- fixef(fit_cc)["neg_100", ]
b_mi <- fixef(fit_mi)[grep("^logpos_mineg", rownames(fixef(fit_mi))), ]
b_lm <- tidy(lm_cc, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term == "neg_100")
b_mice <- pooled |> filter(term == "neg_100")

# Stress test: plug a fixed value into the gap, refit, return the coefficient
sens <- function(fill) {
  d <- cell_data
  d$neg_100[is.na(d$neg_100)] <- fill
  m <- lm(log_pos ~ DPI_f + neg_100, data = d)
  c(estimate = coef(m)[["neg_100"]], confint(m)["neg_100", ])
}
s_lo <- sens(min(cell_data$neg_100, na.rm = TRUE))
s_hi <- sens(max(cell_data$neg_100, na.rm = TRUE))

# One row per approach for the plot
compare <- tibble::tribble(
  ~approach, ~kind, ~est, ~lo, ~hi,
  "brms, complete cases", "Method", b_cc[["Estimate"]], b_cc[["Q2.5"]], b_cc[["Q97.5"]],
  "brms, mi()", "Method", b_mi[["Estimate"]], b_mi[["Q2.5"]], b_mi[["Q97.5"]],
  "lm, complete cases", "Method", b_lm$estimate, b_lm$conf.low, b_lm$conf.high,
  "mice + lm", "Method", b_mice$estimate, b_mice$`2.5 %`, b_mice$`97.5 %`,
  "Fill with smallest", "Stress test", s_lo[[1]], s_lo[[2]], s_lo[[3]],
  "Fill with largest", "Stress test", s_hi[[1]], s_hi[[2]], s_hi[[3]]
) |>
  mutate(approach = factor(approach, levels = rev(approach)))

# Estimate and interval per approach; dashed line at zero (no association)
ggplot(compare, aes(x = est, y = approach, color = kind, shape = kind)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), size = 0.8, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Method = "#0072B2", `Stress test` = "#E69F00")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(Method = 16, `Stress test` = 17)) +
  labs(x = "Coefficient of Pdgfrb_Neg
(log scale, per 100 cells)", y = NULL,
       color = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  Plot_theme +
  legend_top()
```

The six rows tell one story. Every approach puts the coefficient close to `r round(b_cc[["Estimate"]], 2)`, and every interval comfortably includes zero, so on this dataset the data say very little about whether the negative count adds information to the positive count beyond the day. Even the stress tests, which plug in the most extreme values the column has ever shown, move the point estimate by less than the width of its own interval. That is what a 2% missing fraction looks like, and it agrees with the rule of thumb above. The thing to take from the figure is not that the methods are interchangeable (the simulation showed they are not, once the fraction or the mechanism gets worse) but that *for this dataset I do not have to agonize*, and I can say why.

::: {.callout-note title="How to report it"}
**Methods.** One of `r n_rows` animals (2%) had a missing PDGFR-β-negative cell count. We analyzed the data four ways: complete cases (linear model and `brms`), multiple imputation with `mice` (20 imputed datasets, pooled with Rubin's rules) and joint imputation inside the model with `brms` (`mi()`). As sensitivity analyses we replaced the missing value with the smallest and the largest observed count. We assumed the value was missing at random given the day, and we documented that the derived total for that animal had been computed as if the missing count were zero.

**Results.** The coefficient for PDGFR-β-negative cells (change in the log of the positive count per 100 cells) was `r round(b_cc[["Estimate"]], 2)` (95% credible interval `r round(b_cc[["Q2.5"]], 2)` to `r round(b_cc[["Q97.5"]], 2)`) with complete cases, `r round(b_mi[["Estimate"]], 2)` with joint imputation and `r round(b_mice$estimate, 2)` with multiple imputation. The interval included zero in every analysis, and the conclusion did not change with how the missing value was handled.
:::

### What `mi()` actually did to `Td79`

I find the `mi()` approach the most instructive of the four, because it makes the imputation visible. The missing count is not hidden inside a preprocessing step: it is a parameter with a posterior, so we can plot it (@fig-missing-imputed). This is a half-eye, because the *shape* of the posterior is the point here (a wide, lopsided distribution), not just its interval, and I show the seven day-3 animals with an observed `Pdgfrb_Neg` as dots for context (@fig-missing-mice pictures the idea).

![Seven animals measured, one not. Multiple imputation, and `mi()`, don't invent a single mouse; they sketch a cloud of plausible ones.](images/eda-missing-data_seven-mice-one-ghost.png){#fig-missing-mice fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of a wooden bench with seven identical small white mice sitting in a neat row and, at the far end, a cluster of about five faint translucent ochre outlines of a mouse in slightly different sizes and postures."}

```{r}
#| label: fig-missing-imputed
#| fig-cap: "Posterior distribution of the missing `Pdgfrb_Neg` of animal `Td79`, in hundreds of cells, from the `mi()` model. Orange triangles are the observed values for the other day-3 animals. The dashed line marks zero cells."
#| fig-alt: "Half-eye plot of a wide, roughly symmetric distribution centered near 2.7 hundred cells, spanning from below zero to about 6. Seven small orange triangles at the bottom mark the observed day-3 values, which lie between about 0.6 and 5.4. A dashed vertical line sits at zero."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.8

# Posterior draws of the imputed (missing) value
imputed <- as_draws_df(fit_mi) |>
  select(starts_with("Ymi_")) |>
  setNames("value")

# The observed values of the other day-3 animals, for context
observed_d3 <- cell_data |>
  filter(DPI == 3, !is.na(neg_100))

# Half-eye of the imputed value, with the observed animals as triangles below
ggplot(imputed, aes(x = value)) +
  stat_halfeye(.width = c(0.5, 0.95), fill = "#0072B2", color = "black",
               point_interval = "median_qi") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_point(data = observed_d3, aes(x = neg_100, y = -0.03),
             color = "#D55E00", shape = 17, size = 3) +
  labs(x = "Pdgfrb_Neg for Td79 (hundreds of cells)", y = NULL) +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
        axis.line.y = element_blank())
```

Two things stand out, and both are lessons about *assumptions* more than about `Td79`. First, the posterior is wide: the model's best guess is `r round(median(imputed$value) * 100)` negative cells, with a 95% interval from `r round(quantile(imputed$value, 0.025) * 100)` to `r round(quantile(imputed$value, 0.975) * 100)`. That is the honest size of what we know about an animal whose count we never saw, and it is the uncertainty that a single plugged-in value (a mean imputation, say) would have pretended away. Second, and this is the cost of the sub-model: I told the model that `neg_100` is Gaussian, and a Gaussian does not know that a cell count cannot be negative. The share of the posterior below zero is `r round(100 * mean(imputed$value < 0), 1)`%, which is impossible for a count. For a tiny problem it is harmless, but it is the kind of assumption that stops being harmless when a larger fraction of the column is missing, and it is why the next step in a serious analysis would be a sub-model that respects the support of the variable (a log-scale or a count sub-model). In `brms`, `mi()` works only with continuous variables, because Stan cannot sample discrete parameters [@mcelreath2020], so a missing count has to be handled through a continuous approximation or be integrated out.

A last sanity check, as the earlier chapters taught: does the `mi()` model reproduce the data it was fit to? A posterior predictive check on the outcome is the same procedure as in @sec-mcmc-model-checking (@fig-missing-ppc).

```{r}
#| label: fig-missing-ppc
#| fig-cap: "Posterior predictive check for `log(Pdgfrb_Pos)` under the `mi()` model: observed data (dark line) against 100 replicated datasets (light lines)."
#| fig-alt: "Density overlay plot. A dark curve for the observed log counts lies within a bundle of light blue curves drawn from the posterior predictive distribution, which have similar shape and range."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4

# Observed log counts (dark line) against 100 datasets simulated from the mi() model;
# legend in the empty upper-left corner of the panel
pp_check(fit_mi, resp = "logpos", ndraws = 100) +
  labs(x = "log(Pdgfrb_Pos)") +
  Plot_theme +
  legend_inside(0.14, 0.82)
```

The replicated datasets cover the observed density, including the shoulder around 6 and the main peak near 8, and they are a little smoother and wider in the tails than the data, which is what a Gaussian on 49 animals with five day effects tends to do. Good enough for a model whose job here is to compare ways of handling an `NA`, not to be the final word on PDGFR-β counts.

### The frequentist equivalent

With one missing value, the Bayesian and frequentist answers are, for practical purposes, the same, and the reason is worth saying plainly. The complete-case `lm` and the complete-case `brms` fit agree because the priors are weak and the likelihood does the work, as in every single-level model so far [@gelman2020]. The `mice` pooled estimate and the `mi()` estimate agree for a deeper reason: both are doing the same thing under the same assumption (MAR), averaging over the plausible values of the one missing count. Multiple imputation does it by drawing 20 completed datasets and combining them with Rubin's rules, and `mi()` does it by sampling the missing value as a parameter at every iteration of the chain. They are two implementations of one idea, and `mi()`'s advantage is that the uncertainty about the missing value flows into the posterior of every other parameter without a separate pooling step.

Where would they diverge? When there is more to lose. With many missing values, the `brms` sub-model and the `mice` imputation model are two different bets about the missing variable, and they can give different answers. With few animals and a weakly identified sub-model, a frequentist imputation model has nothing to regularize it, whereas a prior on the sub-model's parameters can. And in the MNAR case, no choice among these four rescues you: the Bayesian route is to *model the missingness process itself* explicitly, with assumptions you must state and defend, which is what the stress tests above are a crude, honest first step toward.

## Take home message

We started with one `NA` and a question: accident, clue, or problem? My answer, after looking, is "a bit of all three, in different places." As far as the analysis goes, it was an accident: with 1 row in 49, complete cases, imputation inside `brms`, `mice` and even deliberately extreme fills all gave the same answer, which is what the textbooks predict when the missing fraction is below a few percent. As far as the data goes, it was a clue: the `Pdgfrb_Total` of animal `Td79` equals its `Pdgfrb_Pos`, so the total was computed as if the missing negative count were zero, which means the *derived* column is wrong while looking complete, unless the count really was zero (a possibility that I take up in @sec-missing-data-measurement-error). And that is the problem: any analysis that uses `Pdgfrb_Total`, such as the proportion `Pdgfrb_Pos / Pdgfrb_Total` that @sec-logistic-regression models (and from which it leaves this animal out), gives this animal a share of exactly 100%, and that number is an artifact of how the total was filled in. Checking what is *derived from* a column with an `NA` is the habit I would take from this chapter before any of the packages. The second habit is to ask, before you reach for a tool, whether the value *exists*. A structural `NA`, like the clinical rating that OASIS-1 never collected for most young adults (@sec-missing-structural), cannot be imputed or ignored: it changes who your analysis is about, and the honest response is to change the question or the population and to say so.

The rest is a way of thinking. MCAR, MAR and MNAR are claims about how the values were lost, they cannot be read off the data (certainly not from one missing value), and they are settled by knowing how the experiment was run. Complete cases, multiple imputation and `mi()` are not rival answers; they are different assumptions, and @tbl-missing-options says which. When the missing fraction is tiny, choose the simplest one you can defend and report that you checked the others. When it is not, the choice starts to matter, and then the lab notes matter more than the package. The next chapter, @sec-eda-ggplot, goes back to the thing EDA is really for, which is to *draw* the data.
